title: Generative automation: Fluent work product still needs authority
desc: Extends legal software into substantive generation while preserving lawyer or judicial verification, supervision and responsibility.

kps.k: Generative AI expands legal automation from retrieval and classification to producing substantive work product.
kps.d: The cluster’s core proposition is that probabilistic models can draft, summarise, analyse, extract and reorganise legal material through ordinary-language interfaces. Agentic systems may extend this capability by planning and executing multi-step workflows with tools and limited supervision. This broader scope distinguishes generative AI from established search, predictive coding and other task-specific legal software, although hybrid systems increasingly combine generation with retrieval.

qs.q: Unlike traditional AI, which classifies data and recognises     patterns to make predictions or decisions, GenAI systems create entirely new content.
qs.a: Guide for Using Generative Artificial Intelligence in the Legal Sector · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: GAI tools may assist lawyers in tasks such as legal research, contract review, due diligence, document review, regulatory compliance, and drafting letters, contracts, briefs, and other legal documents.
qs.a: ABA Formal Opinion 512: Generative Artificial Intelligence Tools · Regulators & courts · 2024

kps.k: Task-level evidence supports useful performance, but not general superiority across legal practice.
kps.d: The strongest reported comparative evidence is Vals AI’s evaluation of legal tools against lawyers on specified real-world tasks: all tested tools reportedly outperformed lawyers in document summarisation and transcript analysis, while Harvey Assistant also did so in data extraction, chronology generation, and document review and analysis. Other material reports adoption surveys, experiments and product capabilities, but much of the cluster consists of conceptual explanation, professional guidance, illustrative uses or forecasts rather than measured outcomes. Performance on bounded tasks, exams or demonstrations does not establish reliable handling of open-ended strategy, nuanced reasoning or entire legal roles.

qs.q: We see this in the landmark benchmark study that was published earlier this year by Vals AI, a US-based company that evaluates AI tools.(55) Through a series of real-world tasks, the study compared the performance of four legal AI tools against actual lawyers.
qs.a: The Future of the Legal Profession: A Shared Vision — Opening Address at the Legal Profession Symposium 2025 · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: It also argues that there are aspects of legal writing—including reasoning and performing highly fact- and case-specific detailed analysis— where generative AI will offer little help.
qs.a: Generative Artificial Intelligence and the Practice of Law: Impact, Opportunities, and Risks · Academia · 2024

kps.k: Fluent generation does not itself provide factual or legal authority.
kps.d: Sources repeatedly connect legal unreliability to the technology’s design: models predict plausible sequences from learned patterns rather than independently research, understand or verify propositions. Incomplete, outdated, jurisdictionally irrelevant or biased training material compounds that limitation. The resulting output may mix accurate material with fabricated cases, citations or facts while retaining an authoritative tone. Internet access and retrieval-augmented generation can improve grounding and currency, but retrieval omissions, source-quality problems, misinterpretation of user intent and stochastic generation remain possible.

qs.q: Although they draw upon information contained in large datasets, they are designed to generate content, not to locate information or provide authoritative answers to factual inquiries.
qs.a: Interim Policy on the Use of Artificial Intelligence (New York State Unified Court System) · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: These widely used    resources are “not consistently reliable legal research tools because    they do not always provide the correct answers to legal queries and    may even make up case names and citations when they do not    know the answer to a question.” Id.
qs.a: Al-Hamim v. Star Hearthstone, LLC — First Colorado Appellate Ruling on GAI Hallucinations: Sanctions Declined for a Self-Represented Litigant, with Prospective Warning · Regulators & courts · 2024

kps.k: The debate divides over augmentation, substitution and the pace of transformation.
kps.d: More cautious accounts frame generative AI as a copilot for selected tasks, with lawyers retaining judgment and responsibility. More expansive accounts predict sector-wide transformation, pressure on junior writing-intensive work and eventual professional expectations to use AI. Agentic systems intensify this disagreement because they move from prompted assistance toward autonomous execution. These claims remain prospective: benchmark results cover particular tasks, labour displacement is not demonstrated in the supplied material, and time-specific accounts disagree about whether agentic AI is already present in legal practice.

qs.q: GenAI can augment most, if not all, essential tasks,    ranging from routine tasks, such as preparing first drafts for client responses and    summarising lengthy documents, to supporting more complex tasks like legal research and    contract review.
qs.a: Guide for Using Generative Artificial Intelligence in the Legal Sector · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: Note, we are not suggesting that GenAI is a replacing technology  in the legal context.
qs.a: Becoming, Doing, Being: GenAI and the Promise of Professional Identity in Law · Academia · 2025

kps.k: Professional responsibility remains with the lawyer or judicial officer, making meaningful verification and supervision central.
kps.d: Ethics opinions and court guidance generally apply existing duties rather than creating an AI exception. Users must verify generated citations, summaries, facts and relevance before reliance; understand the tool’s capabilities and autonomy; and preserve independent legal or judicial judgment. Agentic autonomy raises the supervision burden because a system may initiate actions or complete workflows without contemporaneous approval. Guidance therefore draws a firm line between assistance and autopilot: systems should not independently make substantive legal determinations, represent clients, file pleadings or exercise judicial functions.

qs.q: Because generative AI creates content, however, lawyers have an obligation to verify that the citations are correct and that they accurately summarize the cases or other information cited.
qs.a: Joint Formal Opinion 2024-200 — Ethical Issues Regarding the Use of Artificial Intelligence · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: Lawyers have professional obligations – to clients and the Court- to verify and validate any information created by generative Al to ensure its accuracy.
qs.a: Ethics of Artificial Intelligence for the Legal Practitioner · Regulators & courts · 2024

kps.k: Responsible adoption requires tool-specific governance, not a generic rule for all AI products.
kps.d: Risk varies by product, data access, safeguards, jurisdiction and intended use. Practical controls include vendor and security review, restrictions on confidential inputs, clarity over prompt and output rights, checks on whether inputs train third-party systems, documentation of inputs and errors, bias and accuracy review, client communication, liability and insurance assessment, and continuing training. Courts and firms must also distinguish substantive generation from editing, transcription, search and established technology-assisted review. These controls may preserve useful drafting and summarisation benefits without assuming that every tool or use case has the same risk profile.

qs.q: The risks vary based on what product licensees are using; what they are using it for; and what ability the licensee has to mitigate that risk.
qs.a: Licensee use of generative artificial intelligence (White Paper) · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: - review the generative AI vendor’s data management, security and standards.
qs.a: Ethics of Artificial Intelligence for the Legal Practitioner · Regulators & courts · 2024

kps.k: Predicted efficiency, access and business-model gains remain conditional on reliable implementation.
kps.d: Proponents expect faster routine work, lower delivery costs, broader access to legal resources, improved client service and new business models. Rapid public uptake and integration into ordinary office and legal software support expectations of continued adoption, but they do not prove legal effectiveness, lower consumer prices or a reduced justice gap. Realising these benefits depends on task selection, interface and system design, current authoritative data, verification costs, user skill and consumer trust. Some sources therefore urge rapid preparation, while others warn against inflated expectations and direct extrapolation from professional use to courts or consumer-facing systems.

qs.q: Its increasing availability makes it easier for firms to use it to provide services more affordably, effectively and efficiently than before.
qs.a: Risk Outlook Report: The Use of Artificial Intelligence in the Legal Market · Regulators & courts · 2023

qs.q: Generative AI also could reduce the access to justice gap by making legal resources more widely available.
qs.a: ABA Task Force on Law and Artificial Intelligence — Year 1 Report on the Impact of AI on the Practice of Law (August 2024) · Regulators & courts · 2024

vlens.an: The curated academia and research sources collectively accept the proposition’s core distinction: generative AI can produce substantive legal work, but fluent output is not inherently reliable or authoritative. Their common reasoning is that probabilistic generation, incomplete or unsuitable source material, retrieval omissions and the difficulty of open-ended legal reasoning prevent bounded task performance from establishing general legal competence. Several sources therefore favour augmentation, critical evaluation and retained human judgment rather than wholesale substitution. This voice materially develops the proposition by proposing concrete responses: verification-oriented system design, curriculum-wide training in evaluating AI-generated documents, task-specific evaluation methods, and greater attention to whether workers can recognise ineffective assistance. Material variation remains. Some sources directly require verification in litigation, while others discuss only technical capabilities or prospective adoption and therefore leave supervision and responsibility unaddressed. More expansive accounts anticipate agentic workflows, major professional transformation or pressure on junior work, whereas cautious accounts stress non-replacement, interpretive discretion and context-specific deployment. These transformation and labour claims are presented largely as predictions rather than demonstrated outcomes. No supplied source clearly rejects the proposition, so this variation does not make the overall position Mixed.

qs.q: The following section examines a series of legal cases where reliance on GenAI models had serious repercussions, underscoring the risks of treating AI-generated content as authoritative without verifying its accuracy and relevance.
qs.a: The Promise and the Peril of the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Litigation · Academia · 2025

qs.q: It provides examples of exercises where stu- dents learn to collaborate with generative AI, evaluate AI-generated documents, create their own AI tutors and debate partners to assist in their studies, role-play with AI in classroom simulations, and reflect on the responsible use of genera- tive AI in the legal profession.
qs.a: Teaching Law in the Age of Generative AI · Academia · 2024

vlens.an: This curated market-analysis source accepts and materially develops the proposition’s account of generative AI as a broader form of automation. It explains the technological basis for that expansion—general-purpose training, original-content generation, natural-language interaction and increased computing power—and therefore strengthens the cluster’s distinction between generative systems and earlier specialised or predictive methods. It also adds a mechanism for potentially rapid adoption: intuitive interfaces may lower technical barriers. The source does not, however, address the proposition’s equally important legal-specific claims about authoritative grounding, hallucinations, verification, lawyer supervision or professional responsibility. Its adoption claim is predictive rather than proof of sustained adoption or reliable legal performance. Because only one market-analysis source is supplied, no cross-source variation within this professional voice can be established; the material variation within the source is between claims about present technological characteristics and forecasts about their effect on adoption.

vlens.an: The anonymous frontline practitioner supports the cluster’s principal proposition that generative AI can assist with substantive drafting but should not be treated as an authoritative source of legal answers. The source’s reasoning aligns with the cluster’s account of probabilistic language generation and unreliable or outdated training material. Its stance is stricter than the synthesis: rather than accepting answer-oriented uses subject to meaningful verification, it categorically rejects using generative AI to obtain answers. It also does not develop the synthesis’s broader requirements for lawyer supervision, tool-specific governance or retrieval-grounded systems. Because the evidence contains only one anonymous practitioner, it establishes neither a common view among frontline practitioners nor material internal variation within that professional voice.

vlens.an:
The curated regulators, courts and professional bodies support the proposition that generative AI can produce substantive legal work but does not itself supply legal authority, displace professional judgment or remove human responsibility. Their common reasoning is that probabilistic generation can produce persuasive but inaccurate material, especially where training data are incomplete, outdated, biased or jurisdictionally unsuitable. Accordingly, they generally apply existing professional and judicial duties: users must understand the particular tool, verify citations, facts and summaries, protect confidential information, and retain meaningful supervision and independent decision-making.

Material variation concerns emphasis and ambition rather than the proposition’s core. Ethics opinions and court-user guidance focus most directly on verification and accountability; judicial guidance draws a particularly firm boundary against delegating adjudicative functions; other professional reports are more adoption-oriented, stressing possible efficiency, access-to-justice or service-delivery gains while treating them as conditional or prospective. Some sources mainly explain capabilities and risks without fully specifying supervision duties, and one supplied source is too limited to establish a position on the full proposition. The Fifth Circuit materials go further by proposing process-based disclosure even where generated text is not incorporated into a filing. More expansive transformation forecasts also appear, including task-specific benchmark claims and predictions about future professional expectations, but these do not amount to rejection of continued human authority. These patterns describe only the curated sources supplied, not regulators, courts or professional bodies generally.

qs.q: Because generative AI creates content, however, lawyers have an obligation to verify that the citations are correct and that they accurately summarize the cases or other information cited.
qs.a: Joint Formal Opinion 2024-200 — Ethical Issues Regarding the Use of Artificial Intelligence · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: JJOs should ensure that all judicial decisions continue to be independently and personally made by themselves, and should not under any circumstances allow generative AI to take over performance of their judicial functions.
qs.a: Guidelines on the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence for Judges and Judicial Officers and Support Staff of the Hong Kong Judiciary · Regulators & courts · 2024

elens.an: Taken together, the curated 2023–2024 sources support the proposition that generative AI extends legal automation into substantive drafting, summarisation, research and analysis, while fluent output still requires authoritative grounding and retained human responsibility. Common reasons are that models generate statistically plausible content rather than independently establish truth; training data may be incomplete, outdated, jurisdictionally unsuitable or biased; and outputs can therefore include fabricated authorities, inaccurate facts or misleading analysis. Ethics opinions and court guidance consequently apply existing duties of competence, verification and independent judgment, generally treating AI as a copilot rather than an autopilot. Material variation concerns emphasis and evidentiary strength: some sources focus principally on capability, adoption, efficiency, access to justice or business-model forecasts and do not specify verification standards; others impose concrete verification, risk-management or non-delegation requirements. A few materially extend the proposition into process-based disclosure, legal education and tool-specific governance. Claims of transformation, lower costs and broader access remain mostly prospective, while the period’s supplied material contains little comparative task-level evidence and gives limited attention to agentic systems. Two technically descriptive sources do not provide enough legal-governance evidence to establish a position, but they do not counter the period’s overall support.

qs.q: This involves directly producing content, such as contract drafting, client letters or any other form of written communication or document.
qs.a: Risk Outlook Report: The Use of Artificial Intelligence in the Legal Market · Regulators & courts · 2023

qs.q: Because generative AI creates content, however, lawyers have an obligation to verify that the citations are correct and that they accurately summarize the cases or other information cited.

elens.an: The curated 2025 sources broadly support the proposition that generative AI extends legal automation into substantive drafting, summarisation, analysis and related workflows, but that fluent output remains non-authoritative and requires human verification, supervision and responsibility. Common reasons are technical and professional: probabilistic generation can produce plausible but inaccurate material; training and retrieval may be incomplete, outdated, biased or jurisdictionally irrelevant; and lawyers and judicial officers retain duties concerning accuracy, confidentiality and independent judgment. The principal internal variation concerns scale and pace. Some sources extrapolate from Vals AI’s bounded task comparisons and emerging agentic capabilities to sector-wide transformation, junior-work pressure or future expectations to use AI. More cautious sources frame AI as a copilot, stress that task-level or exam performance does not establish general legal competence, and treat efficiency or adoption gains as prospective. Two sources materially extend the proposition: one proposes a verifiable language agent as a system-level remedy, while another develops tacit-knowledge transfer and users’ ability to recognise ineffective assistance. Other sources provide only technical or historical background and therefore leave the governance element unclear. None of this should be read as representative of all 2025 legal or professional opinion.

qs.q: Although they draw upon information contained in large datasets, they are designed to generate content, not to locate information or provide authoritative answers to factual inquiries.
qs.a: Interim Policy on the Use of Artificial Intelligence (New York State Unified Court System) · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.a: Interim Policy on the Use of Artificial Intelligence (New York State Unified Court System) · Regulators & courts · 2025

elens.an:
The curated 2026 sources collectively support the proposition that generative AI extends legal automation into substantive work product but does not thereby acquire factual, legal or professional authority. The clearest support comes from California’s practical guidance: it links probabilistic generation to plausible inaccuracies and fabricated legal citations, and expressly requires meaningful lawyer supervision and review when agentic systems undertake substantive legal activity. The legal-sector guide similarly combines broad drafting, synthesis and analysis capabilities with warnings that outputs may be inaccurate, fictitious or misleading, while framing GenAI as augmentation rather than professional replacement. The Verification-Value Paradox excerpt also preserves human authority by treating predictive outputs as subordinate to lawyers’ experience and judgment.

Material variation concerns scope rather than disagreement. Tellmann’s account extends the automation side of the proposition by forecasting agentic systems that set sub-goals, select tools and execute multi-step actions with minimal supervision, but the supplied excerpt does not address verification or retained professional responsibility. The professional-services research agenda likewise explains generation of professional work product but is silent on authority and safeguards. These sources are therefore unclear on the proposition’s central normative limit rather than opposed to it. Across the period, much of the evidence is conceptual, illustrative or guidance-based; it does not establish general legal performance, professional substitution or realised sector-wide transformation. Because the sources are curated, their alignment should not be treated as evidence of prevalence among regulators, scholars or legal professionals generally.

qs.q: In addition, generative AI may produce outputs that are probabilistic, not deterministic, and may generate plausible but inaccurate information, including purported citations to legal authority that does not exist (frequently called “hallucinations”).
qs.a: Practical Guidance for the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in the Practice of Law · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: Lawyers must not deploy agentic systems in a manner that allows the system to make substantive legal determinations, communicate legal advice, prepare and file pleadings, or otherwise act in a representative capacity without meaningful lawyer supervision 1 and review.
qs.a: Practical Guidance for the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in the Practice of Law · Regulators & courts · 2026
